title: Local communities and Back Heathrow on the draft Heathrow Expansion NPS
label: 13 October 2026 · Heathrow expansion evidence session
summary: Residents’ groups, a regional park representative and Back Heathrow gave the Transport Committee their views on the Government’s draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement (HENPS). Community representatives said the HENPS is vague, lacks enforceable targets and leaves too much to the later Development Consent Order (DCO) process — particularly on noise, ultrafine particle monitoring, compensation, environment and local services. Back Heathrow argued the four tests are appropriately demanding and stressed jobs and local support. Witnesses disagreed on whether the NPS’s designation as ‘critical national growth infrastructure’ would outweigh local harms, and several asked for stronger independent oversight and clearer baselines before any expansion proceeds.

glossary.definition: Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement — the Government’s document setting out the policy tests and expectations for a new runway.
Development Consent Order — the statutory planning process that a major infrastructure promoter must go through for detailed permissions.
Ultrafine particles — airborne particles smaller than 0.1 micrometres, not always measured in planning assessments, with uncertain health effects.
Large noise studies referenced in evidence that assess aircraft noise exposure and impacts; witnesses said their results have been delayed.
A label in the NPS meaning the project is judged nationally important for growth and can override some other planning considerations.
A procedure where property owners can seek compensation if a proposed development makes their property unsaleable or much less valuable.
A legal agreement between a developer and local authority requiring measures (often mitigation or funding) tied to a planning permission.
Regulatory Asset Base model — a way of financing infrastructure through guaranteed returns, which can affect incentives for mitigation spending.

chapters.title: Who was in the room and what they represent
chapters.takeaway: Five local witnesses — three residents’ group members, a regional park manager and Back Heathrow — set out differing priorities: community protections versus jobs and growth.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: This session is scrutiny of the draft Heathrow Expansion NPS. We have two panels; this first panel brings community groups, a regional park representative and Back Heathrow.

turns.speaker: Parmjit Dhanda
turns.text: Back Heathrow is a campaign of about 105,000 local supporters, many connected to the airport by work or supply chains; we want the growth and jobs a new runway can bring.

turns.speaker: Mike Fawcett
turns.text: I represent the Putney Society; our main concern is aircraft noise over Putney and Roehampton, including disturbance at night.

turns.speaker: Christian Hughes
turns.text: I chair Longford Residents’ Association. Our villages are historic neighbours of Heathrow and many residents strongly oppose expansion.

turns.speaker: Deborah Petty
turns.text: I sit on Heathrow’s Noise and Airspace Community Forum for Molesey Residents Association and update Elmbridge Council; I’m here as a volunteer.

turns.speaker: Stewart Pomeroy
turns.text: I manage Colne Valley Regional Park, a charity protecting countryside west of London used by millions nearby; expansion would affect rivers, green belt and public access.

chapters.title: Are the NPS tests clear and enforceable?
chapters.takeaway: Community witnesses said the HENPS is vague and lacks enforcement; Back Heathrow called the tests demanding but supported independent oversight.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The draft HENPS sets four tests that must be met before expansion proceeds. Are those tests right and set at the right level for communities?

turns.speaker: Deborah Petty
turns.text: The HENPS is 'woolly' and toothless. It uses phrases like 'reasonable steps' and 'as far as reasonably practicable', lets the promoter mark its own homework and offers no sanctions or independent checks.

turns.speaker: Deborah Petty
turns.text: It has almost no hard targets beyond a few items (mode share, apprenticeships). Communities need stronger independent assessment, clearer delivery bodies and enforceable metrics on noise and pollutants.

turns.speaker: Christian Hughes
turns.text: I agree. The planning and airspace processes are disjointed; promoters can dismiss costly mitigation. We also need health and vibration monitoring baselines before any change.

turns.speaker: Mike Fawcett
turns.text: The noise 'test' is flawed: it compares to 2024, when noise levels were already high. Holding harm at that level isn't acceptable; averages hide the real impact of new concentrated flight paths.

turns.speaker: Parmjit Dhanda
turns.text: We think the tests are demanding and appropriate. I also support the idea of an independent noise regulator to ensure credible oversight at the DCO stage.

turns.speaker: Stewart Pomeroy
turns.text: Something vital is missing: there is no natural environment test to assess the huge impacts on rivers and ecology; that should be included now, not left to later.

chapters.title: Noise: baselines, change and respite
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses warned that averages and weak metrics hide the disruptive reality of new flight paths and reduced respite; they asked for pre-construction monitoring and stronger protections.

turns.speaker: Mike Fawcett
turns.text: The appraisal shows there will be four streams of traffic over three runways. That means many areas will lose long periods of respite and face planes every two minutes for much of the day.

turns.speaker: Mike Fawcett
turns.text: The key problem is change: people who hardly ever hear aircraft will suddenly have sustained noise. The HENPS’ focus on averages won't capture that concentrated increase.

turns.speaker: Deborah Petty
turns.text: We’ve asked for noise impact studies to include ANAS/ANNE results. Those studies, if included, would show many more people affected — the DfT FOI figures we have suggest 1.9 million could see 25–100% noise increases, and 400,000 might see 100% or more.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What’s the source of those figures?

turns.speaker: Deborah Petty
turns.text: They came from a Department for Transport Freedom of Information request; people deserve to know the scale of potential change.

turns.speaker: Christian Hughes
turns.text: At village level we have sought noise, vibration and ultrafine particle monitoring for years but been refused access to full datasets. We need baselines now so post‑project comparisons are meaningful.

turns.speaker: Parmjit Dhanda
turns.text: Noise affects people differently; many locals say it’s their normal. Still, transparency over flight paths, insulation and compensation is essential and should be clarified early.

chapters.title: Air pollution, green belt and the 'critical national growth' label
chapters.takeaway: Communities argued ultrafine particles, biodiversity and green belt impacts are poorly addressed; the 'critical national growth infrastructure' status risks overriding these concerns, a point fiercely disputed.

turns.speaker: Jacob Collier
turns.text: How well does the HENPS address air pollution and long-term monitoring?

turns.speaker: Christian Hughes
turns.text: UFPs aren't properly covered. Heathrow’s own documents say UFPs near runways have been many times WHO guidelines. The HENPS does not require comprehensive UFP baseline monitoring or data sharing.

turns.speaker: Deborah Petty
turns.text: Local authorities will need funding to provide extra monitors; without that we won’t get accurate, borough‑wide data for particulates or noise.

turns.speaker: Stewart Pomeroy
turns.text: The proposal would take about 1,200 hectares of green belt and displace businesses and houses. The NPS doesn’t adequately consider cumulative impacts on rivers, chalk streams and landscape connectivity.

turns.speaker: Chris Hinchliff
turns.text: Does labelling the project as 'critical national growth infrastructure' risk overriding air, noise and environmental concerns?

turns.speaker: Deborah Petty
turns.text: Yes — it feels like a trump card that could 'stuff' local objections. We also worry the economic case is weak: DfT’s GDP numbers for expansion look modest and Heathrow’s job and GDP claims aren’t fully substantiated in public detail.

turns.speaker: Parmjit Dhanda
turns.text: Locally many people see Heathrow as critical because of jobs and the supply chain. The detailed, statutory scrutiny will come at DCO stage where specifics can be tested.

turns.speaker: Mike Fawcett
turns.text: The tests in HENPS are set so that they could be met without real mitigation; combined with the 'critical' label, that removes incentive to do more to protect communities.

turns.speaker: Stewart Pomeroy
turns.text: If the scheme isn’t affordable, mitigation gets cut. We need a clear master plan for nature, rivers and green space, not piecemeal promises.

chapters.title: Transport, jobs, compensation, heritage and what’s left to the DCO
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses pressed for clearer commitments on surface access, local jobs, compensation and heritage protection; many said too much is being left to the DCO and asked for enforceable baselines and independent checks now.

turns.speaker: Daniel Francis
turns.text: What gives you confidence local communities will benefit long-term from jobs if expansion goes ahead?

turns.speaker: Parmjit Dhanda
turns.text: Over decades Heathrow has provided many local jobs and a large supply chain. Local meetings show people want opportunities and worry about losing them if the hub weakens.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is there hard evidence people would lose jobs if a new runway didn’t go ahead?

turns.speaker: Parmjit Dhanda
turns.text: No single cold study was cited here today; local feeling and workforce patterns are the evidence people point to, but a formal risk assessment would be useful.

turns.speaker: Deborah Petty
turns.text: Heathrow’s headline job numbers aren’t publicly broken down. Past promises on permanent jobs after terminal builds have not been transparently evidenced — we need detail.

turns.speaker: Deborah Petty
turns.text: On transport: an extra 60,000 vehicles a day is not realistic for local roads unless major rail links (southern and western rail) are built in advance. If they’re delayed, most people will still drive.

turns.speaker: Christian Hughes
turns.text: Local services are already thin: in south Hillingdon there are shortages of GP, dentist and pharmacy access. Mental-health referrals in the Heathrow villages have risen sharply; uncertainty about expansion is a real health issue.

turns.speaker: Mike Fawcett
turns.text: About 17,000 people would be displaced by the new boundary and may face higher rents or be forced to move further away, affecting local communities and jobs.

turns.speaker: Alex Mayer
turns.text: What about compensation and heritage? Are residents and historic assets adequately protected?

turns.speaker: Christian Hughes
turns.text: No. Promises have softened: earlier offers of 125% of unblighted value now read as 125% of 'unaffected value' — that’s ambiguous. We also have a 600-year-old barn facing being within 50 metres of a runway with no vibration baseline monitoring in place.

turns.speaker: Parmjit Dhanda
turns.text: The HENPS sets a framework that allows alternatives and compensation where required. But the detailed answers will come in the DCO process and must be rigorous.

turns.speaker: Mike Fawcett
turns.text: Many witnesses here agree: too much important detail is being left to the DCO. Given the likely political stance in favour of expansion, the DCO dynamics will be very different from a normal case.

turns.speaker: Christian Hughes
turns.text: A final point: the easterly alternation decision and the section 106 obligations are treating monitoring as the only mitigation. That mirrors the HENPS approach and means communities are asked to accept 'monitor now, mitigate later'. We need mitigation and baselines before irreversible change.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. The committee may accept brief additional written evidence. We’ll close this panel and move on.
